questions.question: When a node cannot reach a quorum, what is the choice it faces?

options.text: Stay available and risk returning stale data, or refuse service and stay correct
Lose data, or lose durability for writes already acknowledged
Partition the data further, or replicate it more widely
Abort the request, or retry it until the network recovers

questions.explanation: This is the trade-off the chapter spends its length unpacking: linearizability costs availability during a partition, and the two cannot both be had while the network is broken.

questions.question: What is the simplest way of handling faults, and what is the alternative?

options.text: Let the whole service fail and show the user an error message
The simplest way is retrying; the alternative is replication
The simplest way is failover; the alternative is manual repair
The simplest way is logging; the alternative is monitoring

questions.explanation: Fail loudly versus keep working — the chapter is about the second.

questions.question: Which Chapter 8 problems must be assumed to occur? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Packets can be lost, reordered, duplicated, or arbitrarily delayed in the network
Clocks are approximate at best
Nodes can pause for a considerable amount of time or crash at any time
Nodes may lie and send arbitrary faulty responses

questions.explanation: Byzantine behaviour is excluded — the chapter assumes non-Byzantine faults.

questions.question: What is the best way of building fault-tolerant systems, and which pretenses do transactions maintain? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Find some general-purpose abstractions with useful guarantees, implement them once, and then let applications rely on those guarantees
That there are no crashes (atomicity)
That nobody else is concurrently accessing the database (isolation)
That every message sent over the network is eventually delivered (reliability)

questions.explanation: Network reliability is not one of the transaction abstractions listed. The fourth is durability: that storage devices are perfectly reliable. Even though crashes, race conditions, and disk failures do occur, the transaction abstraction hides those problems.

questions.question: Define consensus, and how hard is it to achieve?

options.text: Getting all of the nodes to agree on something
Electing a leader among a set of nodes, which is straightforward with timeouts
Ordering all writes in a replication log, which is solved by Lamport timestamps
Detecting node failures reliably, which turns out to be impossible in an asynchronous network

questions.explanation: Agreement on something, and it is surprisingly tricky.

questions.question: What concrete use of consensus does the opening give?

options.text: To elect a new leader when the old one dies
Deciding which partition a key belongs to
Deciding when to compact SSTables
Deciding the isolation level for a transaction

questions.explanation: Leader election, with split brain as the failure it prevents and data loss as the consequence.

questions.question: Put the three movements of this chapter's argument in order.

options.text: Linearizability, then ordering guarantees, then consensus
Consensus, then linearizability, then ordering
Ordering, then consensus, then linearizability
Transactions, then replication, then partitioning

questions.explanation: The chapter's point is that these are not three separate topics but one.

questions.question: Why map the fundamental limits before reaching for algorithms?

options.text: Because some faults can be tolerated and others cannot
Because algorithms change too often to be worth learning
Because proofs are more useful than implementations
Because the chapter has no space for algorithms

questions.explanation: The chapter also states its self-limitation: it can only scratch the surface, will not go into details of formal models and proofs, and sticks with informal intuitions, pointing to the literature references for depth.

questions.question: Why do you see different data on two database nodes at the same moment, and which replication methods does this affect?

options.text: Because write requests reach different nodes at different times
Because of clock skew; only leaderless replication is affected
Because of partitioning; only multi-leader replication is affected
Because of network faults; only single-leader replication is affected

questions.explanation: Arrival-time differences, and no replication method escapes them.

questions.question: State the definition of eventual consistency exactly, including the two qualifiers readers usually drop.

options.text: Stop writing, wait an unspecified time, and all reads agree
All reads return the latest write within a bounded time
All replicas converge within one second of a write
All reads on the same node return the same value

questions.explanation: You must stop writing, and the waiting time is unspecified. The parenthetical assumption is that any conflicts are resolved. The chapter suggests 'convergence' would be a better name, as we expect all replicas to eventually converge to the same value.

questions.question: What does eventual consistency not promise? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: It doesn't say anything about when the replicas will converge
Until the time of convergence, reads could return anything or nothing
There is no guarantee that you will see the value you just wrote
It does not guarantee that a write, once acknowledged, will be durable

questions.explanation: Three specific complaints. Read-your-writes is separately discussed in Chapter 5.

questions.question: Why is eventual consistency specifically hard for application developers?

options.text: Because a normal single-threaded variable never behaves that way
Because the API it exposes is unfamiliar to most developers
Because it requires manual conflict resolution in every single case
Because its behaviour cannot be tested in any systematic way

questions.explanation: The variable analogy is what makes the weak semantics surprising.

questions.question: Why are weak-guarantee bugs subtle and hard to find by testing?

options.text: Because weak guarantees demand constant vigilance from you
Because such bugs only ever occur in a production environment
Because such bugs always crash the application outright
Because a test suite cannot exercise a real database at all

questions.explanation: Faults and high concurrency are the two conditions that surface them.

questions.question: What do stronger guarantees cost, and what do they buy?

options.text: Worse performance, or less fault tolerance, in exchange for guarantees
They cost only money, and what they buy is correctness
They cost nothing at all, and what they buy is correctness
They cost correctness, and what they buy is performance

questions.explanation: Performance and fault tolerance traded for ease of correct use.

questions.question: How do distributed consistency models relate to transaction isolation levels?

options.text: Mostly independent: isolation is about concurrent writes, this about recency
They are the very same hierarchy described under two different names
Transaction isolation is a special case of distributed consistency
Distributed consistency is a special case of transaction isolation

questions.explanation: Concurrency versus replication — mostly independent, with some overlap.

questions.question: What is the wish that motivates linearizability, and what other names does it go by? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: The wish: to make a system appear as if there were only one replica, so that every client would have the same view of the data and you don't have to worry about replication lag
It is also known as atomic consistency and strong consistency
It is also known as immediate consistency and external consistency
It is simply another name for eventual consistency, used mainly in the academic literature rather than by practitioners

questions.explanation: Four other names in the literature — though the exact definition is quite subtle.

questions.question: Alice and Bob check a football result on their phones; Alice sees the final score and Bob, reloading afterwards, does not. Walk through what happened.

options.text: Alice and Bob check the World Cup final result on their phones
Two clients write conflicting values and the database keeps both
A leader fails and a stale follower is promoted
A transaction reads a partially updated state

questions.explanation: A stale read that is provably stale because of an out-of-band channel.

questions.question: What precisely converts Bob's stale read into a linearizability violation?

options.text: That he reloaded after hearing Alice, so his result should be no older
That the replica he read from was lagging by more than a second
That his two requests were routed to two different replicas
That the final score had already been flushed to disk

questions.explanation: The known ordering between the two reads is what makes the staleness a violation.

questions.question: A single value that can be read and written is called what in the literature, and what could it be in practice?

options.text: A register — a key, a row, or a document
A variable — in practice a table, an index, or a partition
An object — in practice a transaction, a lock, or a lease
A replica — in practice a node, a disk, or a file

questions.explanation: Linearizability is defined over a single register at a time.

questions.question: In Figures 9-2 through 9-4, what do the ends of each bar mean?

options.text: Request sent at the bar's start, response received at its end
The start is when the database processed the request and the end is when it was durable
The start is the transaction begin and the end is the commit
The bars show the duration of the network round-trip only

questions.explanation: A footnote flags a subtle detail: the diagram assumes the existence of a global clock, represented by the horizontal axis. For the purposes of analyzing a distributed algorithm we may pretend an accurate global clock exists, as long as the algorithm doesn't have access to it — the algorithm only gets a mangled approximation of real time, as produced by a quartz oscillator and NTP.

questions.question: x is initially 0 and client C writes 1 while A and B poll. Which readings are permitted? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: A read that completes before the write begins must return the old value 0
A read that begins after the write has completed must return the new value 1
A read that overlaps the write in time may return either 0 or 1, because we don't know whether the write has taken effect at the point when the read is processed — these operations are concurrent
A read whose bar overlaps the write must nonetheless return 1, because the write has already been sent by then

questions.explanation: Rule (c) alone is insufficient: it permits the value to flip back and forth between old and new across successive reads. A footnote notes that a register that allows exactly that is called a regular register.

questions.question: Beyond read and write, what extra constraint does linearizability place on concurrent reads of the same value?

options.text: Once one read returns the new value, every later read must too
That every read must be served from the leader node
That every write must be replicated synchronously
That two concurrent reads must return the same value

questions.explanation: This is the constraint that rules out flip-flopping.

questions.question: Define the compare-and-set operation.

options.text: Compare-and-set, which updates only if the old value still matches
Increment-and-get, which adds one and returns the new value
Read-modify-write, which is not an atomic operation
Append, which adds an entry to the end of a log

questions.explanation: Compare-and-set is the operation that later turns out to require consensus.

questions.question: When is an operation taken to have executed, and what must the resulting order satisfy?

options.text: A vertical line inside each bar, marking when it took effect
They mark the request send time; the lines may move backward
They mark durability; the lines are unordered
They mark network arrival; the lines must be evenly spaced

questions.explanation: Forward-only ordering ensures the recency guarantee: once a new value has been written or read, all subsequent reads see the value that was written, until it is overwritten again.

questions.question: B sends its read first, then D sets x = 0, then A sets x = 1 — yet B's read returns 1. Why is that still linearizable?

options.text: Because D's write, then A's write, then B's read is a valid order
Because reads are always served directly from the leader
The ordering shown is not legal at all, and the figure is marking it as a linearizability violation
Because B's read carried a later timestamp than the write

questions.explanation: Concurrent requests may be processed in any order, including one that differs from send order.

questions.question: B's read returns 1 before client A receives its ok confirming the write of 1. Why is this not a violation?

options.text: Because the ok response merely arrived slightly later on the network
Because reads and writes are entirely independent operations
Because client B happened to read from a different replica
It is a violation, and the figure marks it as one

questions.explanation: The response delay is on the network, not in the execution order.

questions.question: Linearizability does not assume transaction isolation. How does that show up, and which compare-and-set requests succeed?

options.text: Because B changed the value between C's two reads
All three of the cas requests succeed in turn
Only client D's cas request succeeds
All three of the cas requests fail outright

questions.explanation: No isolation means an intervening write can invalidate the compare.

questions.question: Which single operation in a linearizability diagram can be non-linearizable, and why?

options.text: The final read by client B, shown in a shaded bar
D's cas, because it returned an error
A's write of 1, because it overlapped D's write of 0
C's first read of 1, because it preceded the write

questions.explanation: Once a newer value has been read by anyone, no later read may go back. Testing for linearizability is possible but computationally expensive: you record the timings of all requests and responses and check whether they can be arranged into a valid sequential order.

questions.question: From the 'Linearizability Versus Serializability' box, define serializability.

options.text: An isolation property covering multiple objects per transaction
It is a recency guarantee on a single register
It requires the serial order to match the real-time order
It applies to single-object operations only

questions.explanation: Multiple objects, some serial order, and the order need not match reality.

questions.question: From the same box, define linearizability and name the anomaly it doesn't prevent.

options.text: A recency guarantee on reads and writes of one object
It prevents write skew between transactions automatically
It groups several operations together into transactions
It applies across multiple objects rather than one

questions.explanation: Single object, recency only — write skew spans objects and so escapes it.

questions.question: What is the combination of serializability and linearizability called, and which implementations provide it?

options.text: Strict serializability, or strong one-copy serializability
Strong eventual consistency, provided by serializable snapshot isolation
Snapshot serializability, provided by multi-version concurrency control
Atomic serializability, provided by two-phase commit protocols

questions.explanation: 2PL and serial execution give both; SSI does not.

questions.question: Which serializability implementation is not linearizable, and why by design?

options.text: Serializable snapshot isolation, which reads from a snapshot
Two-phase locking, because locks are released early
Serial execution, because it runs on one thread
All serializable implementations are linearizable

questions.explanation: A consistent snapshot deliberately excludes recent writes, which is exactly what linearizability forbids.

questions.question: Which properties belong to linearizability rather than serializability? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: It is a recency guarantee
It concerns a single object or register
It is an isolation property of transactions spanning multiple objects
Its serial order may differ from the real execution order

questions.explanation: The last two belong to serializability. The chapter notes the words are easily confused, as both seem to mean 'can be arranged in a sequential order' — but they are two quite different guarantees.

questions.question: Describe the lock-based leader election scheme and its requirement.

options.text: Every node tries to acquire the lock; the winner leads
The node with the lowest ID becomes leader; no lock is needed
All nodes become leaders and resolve conflicts later
The lock may be eventually consistent

questions.explanation: Without agreement on ownership, the lock provides nothing.

questions.question: Which coordination services provide linearizable operations, and what is built on top of them?

options.text: Apache ZooKeeper and etcd
Redis and Memcached, with Curator on top
Consul and Kafka, with ZooKeeper on top
Cassandra and Riak, with Helix on top

questions.explanation: A footnote adds the fine print: strictly speaking ZooKeeper and etcd provide linearizable writes, but reads may be stale since by default they can be served by any one of the replicas — in etcd you can request a quorum read, and in ZooKeeper you need to call sync() before the read.

questions.question: Describe distributed locking in Oracle Real Application Clusters.

options.text: A lock per disk page, with nodes sharing one storage system
It takes a lock per table, acquired over the public network
It takes a lock per transaction, with no shared storage at all
It takes no locks, relying on multi-version concurrency control

questions.explanation: Page-granularity locks on the critical path force a dedicated interconnect.

questions.question: Give examples of uniqueness constraints, and say when linearizability becomes necessary for them.

options.text: A username or email address, and a file path in a storage service
Foreign key constraints; linearizability is needed for all constraints
Range constraints; linearizability is never needed
Check constraints; linearizability is needed only on read

questions.explanation: Enforcement at write time is what requires linearizability.

questions.question: How is registering a username best understood?

options.text: As acquiring a lock on the chosen username
As a foreign key reference to the accounts table
As an eventual-consistency merge between replicas
As a read-only query with no side effects

questions.explanation: Lock and compare-and-set are two framings of the same requirement.

questions.question: Which further constraints reduce to uniqueness, and what property do they share? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: A bank account balance never going negative
Not selling more items than you have in stock
Two people not concurrently booking the same seat on a flight or in a theater
Referential integrity between two tables in the same database

questions.explanation: These constraints all require there to be a single up-to-date value — the account balance, the stock level, the seat occupancy — that all nodes agree on.

questions.question: Give an example of a constraint that can be treated loosely.

options.text: When the application can handle the violation after the fact
Bank balances, which can go negative temporarily with no consequence
Usernames, which can be duplicated and merged
File paths, which can collide safely

questions.explanation: Compensatable violations don't need prevention. The chapter draws a sharp line: a hard uniqueness constraint such as the one typically found in relational databases requires linearizability, whereas other kinds of constraints such as foreign key or attribute constraints can be implemented without requiring linearizability.

questions.question: In that football-result example, what would have happened if Alice had said nothing?

options.text: That Bob would never have known his result was stale
The database would have detected and reported the staleness
Bob would have seen the correct result
The replica would have blocked the read

questions.explanation: Without the out-of-band channel, staleness is undetectable to the client.

questions.question: Describe the photo-upload and resizing architecture, and why the image itself isn't put on the queue.

options.text: A web server takes uploads and a background resizer makes thumbnails
The photo is placed on the queue because brokers handle large messages well
The photo is written to the resizer's local disk
There is no message queue involved; the web server calls the resizer synchronously and waits for it

questions.explanation: Two channels — file storage and message queue — is what creates the race.

questions.question: If the file storage service in that architecture is not linearizable, what can go wrong?

options.text: The queue may outrun the storage service's internal replication
The queue message is lost, so the photo is never resized at all
The photo is resized twice over, wasting processing capacity
The resizer retries until it succeeds, so nothing goes wrong

questions.explanation: Permanent inconsistency is what distinguishes this from Alice's self-correcting reload.

questions.question: State the general shape of the cross-channel problem and the alternative to linearizability.

options.text: Because there are two channels: the file storage and the queue
The problem is queue latency; the alternative is a faster broker
The problem is storage durability; the alternative is more replicas
Linearizability is the only possible remedy for this situation

questions.explanation: Simplest to understand, not the only option.

questions.question: What is the simplest implementation of linearizability, and why is it rejected?

options.text: That it behaves as though there is one copy, atomically updated
To use synchronous replication to all replicas; rejected for latency
To use a quorum; rejected for complexity
To use timestamps; rejected for clock skew

questions.explanation: Fault tolerance is what forces replication, which is what makes linearizability hard.

questions.question: Why is single-leader replication only 'potentially' linearizable?

options.text: Because reads from the leader or synchronous followers can be linearizable
Because a leader always lags behind its own followers under load
Because single-leader replication cannot be made linearizable at all
Because reads must always be directed to the followers, never the leader

questions.explanation: Design choices and bugs both break it in practice.

questions.question: What assumption does using the leader for reads rest on, and what breaks it?

options.text: That you know for certain which node is the leader
It relies on clock synchronization, which NTP breaks
It relies on quorum size, which rebalancing breaks
It relies on the leader's disk, which crashes break

questions.explanation: Two failure modes: the delusional leader, and lost writes on failover.

questions.question: Why are consensus algorithms listed as flatly linearizable?

options.text: Because they resemble single-leader replication with split-brain protection
Because they replicate synchronously to every node in the cluster
Because they rely on tightly synchronized clocks between nodes
Because they avoid having a leader node altogether

questions.explanation: Split-brain prevention plus stale-replica prevention is the difference from plain single-leader replication.

questions.question: Why is multi-leader replication not linearizable?

options.text: Because writes are accepted on several nodes and replicated asynchronously
Because their leaders are elected by a proper consensus algorithm
Because writes are replicated synchronously across the datacenters
Because their reads are always served from followers rather than leaders

questions.explanation: Multiple write-accepting copies contradicts the single-copy illusion by construction.

questions.question: Which things undermine linearizability in Dynamo-style leaderless systems? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Last write wins conflict resolution methods based on time-of-day clocks, as in Cassandra, are almost certainly nonlinearizable, because clock timestamps cannot be guaranteed to be consistent with actual event ordering due to clock skew
Sloppy quorums also ruin any chance of linearizability
Even with strict quorums, nonlinearizable behavior is possible
Read repair, which always restores linearizability by the time the next read is served

questions.explanation: Depending on the exact configuration of the quorums, and on how you define strong consistency, the claim that quorums give strong consistency is not quite true. A footnote notes that partitioning a single-leader database with a separate leader per partition does not affect linearizability, since it is only a single-object guarantee — though cross-partition transactions are a different matter.

questions.question: A write goes to all three replicas while a read takes two of them, w plus r exceeds n, and yet the read is stale. How?

options.text: A write to all three replicas, concurrent with reads from two
The quorum condition is violated, which explains the anomaly
Both clients read the same value, so there is no anomaly
The writer only wrote to two replicas

questions.explanation: The quorum condition is satisfied and linearizability still fails, because of variable network delays.

questions.question: What makes strict quorums linearizable, at what cost, and what do Riak and Cassandra do?

options.text: Yes, at reduced performance, with synchronous read repair
Both Riak and Cassandra perform synchronous read repair and are linearizable
Neither of the two operations can be made linearizable under any configuration of w and r
Only asynchronous read repair is needed, at no cost

questions.explanation: Synchronous repair on the read path and a read-before-write on the write path.

questions.question: Which operation cannot be made linearizable by these quorum techniques?

options.text: Compare-and-set
Read, which requires consensus
Write, which requires a leader
All three operations can be made linearizable

questions.explanation: Compare-and-set is the operation that crosses the line into consensus.

questions.question: In a two-datacenter deployment with the inter-datacenter link down, what happens under multi-leader replication?

options.text: Each datacenter keeps operating, since replication is asynchronous
Both datacenters become unavailable for writes
One datacenter is elected leader and the other becomes read-only
All writes are rejected until the link recovers

questions.explanation: The figure's caption: a network interruption forcing a choice between linearizability and availability.

questions.question: Same interruption, single-leader setup. What happens?

options.text: The leader sits in one datacenter, and all linearizable traffic goes there
Both of the datacenters continue to accept writes normally
The follower datacenter is promoted to leader automatically
Reads fail while writes succeed in both of the datacenters

questions.explanation: Availability survives only where the leader is reachable.

questions.question: State the CAP trade-off in two bullets, and how wide is its scope?

options.text: They cannot process requests while disconnected, so they must wait or error
The trade-off applies only to multi-datacenter deployments
The trade-off applies only to leaderless replication schemes
The trade-off can be avoided by replicating synchronously

questions.explanation: A footnote gives the labels CP — consistent but not available under network partitions — and AP — available but not consistent under network partitions — but notes the classification scheme has several flaws, so it is best avoided.

questions.question: Attribute the CAP theorem, and give its prehistory.

options.text: Eric Brewer, in 2000
It was proved by Gilbert and Lynch in 2000, with no prehistory
It was named by Brewer in 1990 and proved in 1970
It originates with Codd's relational paper

questions.explanation: Named in 2000, known since the 1970s.

questions.question: What was CAP originally proposed as, and what is it nonetheless worth?

options.text: As a rule of thumb, to start a discussion about trade-offs
It was proposed as a formal theorem with precise definitions from the start
It was proposed as a product benchmark
It had no influence on database design

questions.explanation: A rule of thumb whose main contribution was a culture shift.

questions.question: Why does the 'Unhelpful CAP Theorem' box reject 'pick 2 out of 3'?

options.text: Because a partition is a fault, and faults are not optional
Because you can in fact pick all three of the properties
Because consistency and availability turn out to be the same thing
Because the formulation is too technical to be useful

questions.explanation: You don't choose whether partitions happen, only what to do when they do.

questions.question: What better phrasing does the box offer?

options.text: Both are available while the network works; a partition forces the choice
Consistency, Availability, Partition tolerance: pick any two
Choose availability always, since partitions are rare
Choose consistency always, since correctness matters most

questions.explanation: Both when healthy; a forced choice when partitioned.

questions.question: What is the box's second objection, about availability?

options.text: That the definitions of availability are contradictory
That availability cannot be measured in any meaningful way
That availability is the same as durability
That availability requires linearizability

questions.explanation: The word does not mean in CAP what it means colloquially.

questions.question: How narrow is the formally defined CAP theorem?

options.text: Very narrow: one consistency model and one kind of fault
It covers every consistency model and every kind of fault
It covers the trade-off between latency and throughput
It covers Byzantine faults as well as network partitions

questions.explanation: A footnote disambiguates 'partition': the book normally uses partitioning to mean deliberately breaking down a large dataset into smaller ones (sharding), whereas a network partition is a particular type of network fault, which the book doesn't normally consider separately from other kinds of faults — but since it's the P in CAP, the confusion is unavoidable here.

questions.question: What is the final verdict on CAP?

options.text: Little practical value for designing systems today
CAP remains the primary design tool for distributed systems
CAP has been proved false
CAP applies only to NoSQL databases

questions.explanation: Historically influential, practically superseded.

questions.question: Give the most surprising example of a system that is not linearizable.

options.text: Even RAM on a multi-core CPU is not linearizable
A single-node relational database with serializable isolation
An in-memory key-value store on one machine
A file system on a local disk

questions.explanation: Every CPU core has its own memory cache and store buffer: memory access first goes to the cache by default, and changes are asynchronously written out to main memory. Since accessing data in the cache is much faster than going to main memory, this is essential for good performance — but it means there are several copies of the data, one in main memory and perhaps several more in various caches, which are updated asynchronously, so linearizability is lost.

questions.question: Why is it wrong to invoke CAP to justify the multi-core memory consistency model?

options.text: Because within one computer we assume reliable communication
Because CAP applies only to databases and never to CPUs
Because CPU caches are always linearizable by design
Because a CPU's cores cannot be partitioned from each other

questions.explanation: Performance, not fault tolerance. The same is true of many distributed databases that choose not to provide linearizable guarantees: they do so primarily to increase performance, not so much for fault tolerance. The chapter's blunt one-liner: linearizability is slow — and this is true all the time, not only during a network fault.

questions.question: State the Attiya and Welch bound and its consequences.

options.text: Response time proportional to the uncertainty of delay in the network
They prove that linearizability is outright impossible in an asynchronous network
They prove linearizability costs a constant factor of two
They prove linearizability is free on reliable networks

questions.explanation: Proportional to delay uncertainty, and no faster algorithm exists. Chapter 12 returns to approaches for avoiding linearizability without sacrificing correctness.

questions.question: How does the definition of a linearizable register lead to a statement about ordering?

options.text: Because every operation must appear atomic on a single copy
Because linearizability requires synchronized clocks, which impose order
Because linearizability requires a leader, who imposes order
Linearizability says nothing about order

questions.explanation: Atomic single points in time compose into a single total order.

questions.question: In which earlier contexts has ordering already come up? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Chapter 5: the main purpose of the leader in single-leader replication is to determine the order of writes in the replication log — if there is no single leader, conflicts can occur due to concurrent operations

Chapter 7: serializability is about ensuring that transactions behave as if they were executed in some sequential order, achieved either by literally executing them serially or by allowing concurrent execution while preventing serialization conflicts
Chapter 8: the use of timestamps and clocks in distributed systems is an attempt to introduce order into a disorderly world, for example to determine which of two writes happened later
Chapter 3: index ordering, which determines the order in which key lookups return their results

questions.explanation: Ordering has been a recurring theme in the book, which suggests it might be an important fundamental idea.

questions.question: Give the Consistent Prefix Reads example and the term for the relationship involved.

options.text: An observer who saw the answer before the question
Two writers set the same key; the term is conflict
A reader sees a stale value; the term is read skew
A write is lost on failover; the term is durability

questions.explanation: Causal dependency is the relationship that ordering must respect.

questions.question: Between three leaders, some writes overtake others due to network delays. Which causal rule does that violate?

options.text: Writes overtaking each other between three leaders
Two leaders write conflicting values, violating uniqueness
A leader fails and loses writes, violating durability
A follower lags, violating monotonic reads

questions.explanation: Create-before-update is a causal dependency that arrival order can invert.

questions.question: For two operations A and B, what are the three possibilities?

options.text: A happened before B, B before A, or the two are concurrent
Either A is before B or B is before A, since concurrency cannot arise
Either they conflict or they don't
Either they are on the same node or different nodes

questions.explanation: Three possibilities, of which the third is what makes causality a partial order.

questions.question: What does 'consistent' mean in 'consistent snapshot'?

options.text: Consistent with causality: an answer implies its question
It means that all of the replicas agree on the snapshot
It means that the snapshot itself is linearizable
It means the snapshot contains no concurrent writes

questions.explanation: Causal consistency is the precise sense of 'consistent' here.

questions.question: Show write skew as a causality story, and how SSI exploits it.

options.text: Each transaction thought the other doctor was still on call
Both wrote the same object, so this is a lost update
Both read stale values, so this is read skew
Write skew has no causal interpretation at all

questions.explanation: The premise-and-write pattern is a causal dependency, which is exactly what SSI tracks.

questions.question: Restate the Alice/Bob football violation in the language of causality.

options.text: Bob's stale read after hearing Alice's exclamation
It is a pure concurrency violation with no causal element
It is a durability violation rather than a causal one
It is an instance of write skew between two readers

questions.explanation: The out-of-band channel creates the causal dependency the database cannot see.

questions.question: What orderings does causality impose, and what is the causal order?

options.text: Cause before effect, send before receive, question before answer
Only that writes must come before the reads that follow
Only that earlier timestamps precede later timestamps
Only that a leader's operations precede its followers'

questions.explanation: Chains of dependent operations, not clock readings.

questions.question: Define causal consistency and give an example system providing it.

options.text: Causally consistent
Causal consistency means all reads return the latest write; provided by linearizability only
Causal consistency means replicas converge; provided by eventual consistency
Causal consistency means writes are ordered by timestamp; provided by LWW

questions.explanation: Snapshot isolation's causal consistency is what makes its snapshots meaningful.

questions.question: Define total order and partial order, with an example of each.

options.text: That any two elements can be compared
A partial order allows any two elements to be compared; a total order does not
Both allow all comparisons; they differ in direction
Incomparable elements can still be compared under a total order

questions.explanation: A set is greater than another if it contains all the other's elements.

questions.question: Which consistency model gives a total order and which a partial order?

options.text: A total order, since it behaves as if there were one copy
Causality gives a total order while linearizability gives a partial one
Both causality and linearizability give total orders
Both causality and linearizability give partial orders

questions.explanation: According to this definition there are no concurrent operations in a linearizable datastore: there must be a single timeline along which all operations are totally ordered. There might be several requests waiting to be handled, but the datastore ensures that every request is handled atomically at a single point in time, acting on a single copy of the data along a single timeline without any concurrency.

questions.question: What does concurrency look like drawn as a picture?

options.text: That the timeline branches and merges, leaving incomparable operations
Concurrency is a single line with gaps; the illustration is a replication log
Concurrency is a circle; the illustration is a ring topology
Concurrency cannot be illustrated

questions.explanation: Branch-and-merge is the shape of a partial order.

questions.question: State the relationship between linearizability and causality.

options.text: Linearizability implies causality
Causality implies linearizability rather than the other way round
The two properties are unrelated, so neither implies the other
The two properties are exactly equivalent to one another

questions.explanation: One direction only — linearizability is strictly stronger. But the cost is that making a system linearizable can harm its performance and availability, especially if the system has significant network delays, for example if it's geographically distributed — which is why some distributed data systems have abandoned linearizability, allowing better performance but potentially making them difficult to work with.

questions.question: What is the good news about causal consistency?

options.text: That a system can be causally consistent without linearizability's cost
Causal consistency is a weaker guarantee than eventual consistency
Causal consistency requires linearizability to be used internally
Causal consistency is the strongest consistency model of them all

questions.explanation: Research is exploring this direction, developing databases that preserve causality with performance and availability characteristics similar to eventually consistent systems — but it is quite recent, not much of it has yet made its way into production systems, and there are still challenges to be overcome, though it is a promising direction for future systems.

questions.question: What must a replica do when processing operations, in order to maintain causality?

options.text: Which operation happened before which other operation
It must process all operations in timestamp order
It must process all operations in arrival order
It may process operations in any order at all

questions.explanation: Wait for missing predecessors is the mechanism.

questions.question: To determine causal dependencies, what has to be describable — and what everyday notion captures it?

options.text: The knowledge a node had at the time it issued a write
Wall-clock timestamps; the analogy is a stopwatch
Network topology; the analogy is a map
Quorum membership; the analogy is a vote

questions.explanation: Knowledge, not timing, is what causality tracks.

questions.question: What does causal consistency require beyond leaderless conflict detection?

options.text: Those used in Detecting Concurrent Writes, with version vectors
It requires only per-key tracking, exactly as conflict detection does
It requires clocks that are synchronized across the nodes
It requires a single leader to sequence every operation

questions.explanation: Whole-database scope rather than per-key scope.

questions.question: Why must the database know which version of the data the application read?

options.text: Which version of the data the application read
In order to compute the current replication lag
In order to choose which replica to read from
In order to decide which isolation level applies

questions.explanation: Passing the read version back is the mechanism in both places.

questions.question: What is the practical objection to tracking all causal dependencies?

options.text: Because clients read a lot before writing, making the metadata large
It requires synchronized clocks, which are not available
It requires a single leader, which limits write throughput
The objection does not really hold, since the causal metadata stays small and cheap

questions.explanation: Which motivates sequence numbers as a cheaper approximation.

questions.question: Define a logical clock and its properties.

options.text: Sequence numbers or timestamps from a logical clock
A logical clock is a synchronized physical clock with bounded error
A logical clock measures elapsed time in nanoseconds
A logical clock is a vector of per-node timestamps only

questions.explanation: Compact, totally ordered, and independent of physical time.

questions.question: State the promise of 'a total order that is consistent with causality', and the concession.

options.text: A total order consistent with causality
It guarantees concurrent operations are left unordered
It captures less causality information than a partial order
It imposes exactly the ordering required by causality

questions.explanation: A footnote gives a useless counterexample: you could generate a random UUID for each operation and compare UUIDs lexicographically to define a total order of operations — that is a valid total order, but the random numbers tell you nothing about which operation actually happened first, or whether the operations were concurrent. A total order that is inconsistent with causality is easy to create, but not very useful.

questions.question: How does a single-leader database get a causally consistent total order for free?

options.text: The replication log defines a total order consistent with causality
By synchronizing all of the node clocks using NTP
By attaching a version vector to every single write
It cannot — single-leader replication is not causally consistent

questions.explanation: A single sequencing point gives causality for free, even to laggards.

questions.question: How can sequence numbers be generated without a single leader? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Each node can generate its own independent set of sequence numbers — for example with two nodes, one can generate only odd numbers and the other only even numbers. More generally you can reserve some bits in the binary representation of the sequence number to contain a unique node identifier, ensuring that two different nodes can never generate the same sequence number

You can attach a timestamp from a time-of-day clock (physical clock) to each operation: such timestamps are not sequential, but if they have sufficiently high resolution they might be sufficient to totally order operations — a fact used in the last write wins conflict resolution method

You can preallocate blocks of sequence numbers: node A might claim the block of sequence numbers from 1 to 1,000, and node B might claim the block from 1,001 to 2,000, so each node can independently assign sequence numbers from its block and allocate a new block when its supply begins to run low
Each node can use a random UUID, which happens to order consistently with causality

questions.explanation: Three methods, all of which scale better than pushing all operations through a single leader.

questions.question: What is the common defect of all three generators, and the specific arguments? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: The sequence numbers they generate are not consistent with causality: they do not correctly capture the ordering of operations across different nodes — although each gives a unique, approximately increasing sequence number for each operation

With the odd/even split, one node may end up processing a different number of operations per second than the other, so the counter for even numbers may lag behind the counter for odd numbers, or vice versa — and if you have an odd-numbered operation and an even-numbered operation you cannot accurately tell which one causally happened first
With physical clock timestamps, clock skew means a causally later operation can be assigned a lower timestamp, as in Figure 8-3
With the block allocator, an operation that causally happened later always receives the higher of the two sequence numbers

questions.explanation: The block allocator has the same defect as the others: an operation that causally happened later may be assigned a sequence number in a lower block, because blocks are handed out per node. A footnote notes it is possible to make physical clock timestamps consistent with causality: Google's Spanner estimates the expected clock skew and waits out the uncertainty interval before committing a write, ensuring that a causally later transaction is given a greater timestamp — but most clocks cannot provide the required uncertainty metric.

questions.question: Attribute Lamport timestamps and describe their structure.

options.text: Leslie Lamport, in 1978
Proposed in 1998 by Lamport; a single integer counter per system
Proposed in 1978; a vector of counters, one per node
Proposed in 1985; a wall-clock timestamp plus a node ID

questions.explanation: A pair, compared by counter first and node ID as tiebreak.

questions.question: What is 'the key idea about Lamport timestamps' that makes them consistent with causality?

options.text: Every node and client tracks the maximum counter value it has seen
Each node increments its counter only for its own local operations
Each node synchronizes its counter against an NTP server
Each node resets its counter at the start of every request

questions.explanation: In Figure 9-8, client A receives a counter value of 5 from node 2 and then sends that maximum of 5 to node 1. At that time node 1's counter was only 1, but it was immediately moved forward to 5, so the next operation had an incremented counter value of 6.

questions.question: Distinguish Lamport timestamps from version vectors.

options.text: Version vectors distinguish concurrency; Lamport timestamps force a total order
They are the same mechanism described under two names
Lamport timestamps detect concurrency while version vectors give a total order
Version vectors are more compact than Lamport timestamps

questions.explanation: Total order versus concurrency detection, compactness versus information.

questions.question: Set up the username problem and the apparently sufficient Lamport-timestamp solution.

options.text: Two users concurrently claiming the same username
Version vectors are needed rather than Lamport timestamps
Physical timestamps are sufficient
The problem cannot be solved by any ordering

questions.explanation: After-the-fact resolution works; real-time decision-making does not.

questions.question: Why is 'after the fact' not good enough, and what makes the fix unacceptable?

options.text: When a node must decide right now, without knowing the final order
The timestamps are not comparable, so no decision can be reached
The fix requires clocks synchronized across the cluster
It is already good enough, so no fix is needed at all

questions.explanation: The root problem: the total order of operations only emerges after you have collected all of the operations. If another node has generated some operations but you don't yet know what they are, you cannot construct the final ordering, because unknown operations from the other node may need to be inserted at various positions in the total order.

questions.question: What extra thing do you need beyond a total ordering?

options.text: You also need to know when that order is finalized
You need synchronized clocks with bounded error
You need version vectors as well as Lamport timestamps
You need nothing more; the total order suffices

questions.explanation: Finality, not just order, is the missing requirement.

questions.question: How does single-leader replication produce a total order, and what two challenges follow?

options.text: Choose one node as leader and sequence everything on one core
By synchronizing clocks; the challenges are drift and skew
By quorum voting; the challenges are latency and availability
By version vectors; the challenges are size and comparison

questions.explanation: A footnote objects that 'atomic broadcast' is a confusing term because it is inconsistent with other uses of the word atomic: it has nothing to do with atomicity in ACID transactions and is only indirectly related to atomic operations or atomic registers. Total order multicast is another synonym.

questions.question: Give total order broadcast's two safety properties.

options.text: Reliable delivery, and totally ordered delivery
Bounded delivery and ordered acknowledgment
At-most-once delivery and causal ordering
Exactly-once delivery and timestamp ordering

questions.explanation: A correct algorithm for total order broadcast must ensure the reliability and ordering properties are always satisfied, even if a node or the network is faulty: of course messages will not be delivered while the network is interrupted, but an algorithm can keep retrying so that the messages get through when the network is eventually repaired, and then they must still be delivered in the correct order.

questions.question: Which systems implement total order broadcast, and what does that suggest?

options.text: ZooKeeper and etcd
Kafka and RabbitMQ — a hint about message queues
Cassandra and Riak — a hint about leaderless replication
PostgreSQL and MySQL — a hint about replication logs

questions.explanation: The systems that implement consensus are exactly the ones that implement total order broadcast.

questions.question: Why is total order broadcast exactly what you need for database replication?

options.text: Because every replica applying the same writes in the same order stays consistent
Because it guarantees a bounded amount of replication lag between nodes
Because it removes the need for any leader node in the system
Because it makes every write naturally idempotent on replay

questions.explanation: Similarly, it can implement serializable transactions: if every message represents a deterministic transaction to be executed as a stored procedure, and if every node processes those messages in the same order, then the partitions and replicas of the database are kept consistent with each other.

questions.question: What property about when the order is fixed makes total order broadcast stronger than timestamp ordering?

options.text: The order is fixed when the messages are delivered, not retroactively
The order is fixed at send time rather than at delivery time
The order is never fixed, which is what makes it flexible
The order is fixed by timestamps, making the two equivalent

questions.explanation: Finality at delivery is precisely what Lamport timestamps lack.

questions.question: How does total order broadcast implement a lock service with fencing tokens?

options.text: Append every lock request to the log and let the first one win
Locks are granted by timestamp comparison, with the timestamp as the token
Locks require a separate consensus round per acquisition
Total order broadcast cannot implement locks

questions.explanation: Log position doubles as a monotonic fencing token.

questions.question: Is linearizability the same as total order broadcast?

options.text: Not quite — broadcast is asynchronous, linearizability is a recency guarantee
Yes — the two are exactly identical in what they guarantee
No — the two concepts are unrelated, and neither implies the other
Total order broadcast is the recency guarantee, and linearizability is asynchronous

questions.explanation: A footnote ranks them formally: a linearizable read-write register is an 'easier' problem, because total order broadcast is equivalent to consensus, which has no deterministic solution in the asynchronous crash-stop model, whereas a linearizable read-write register can be implemented in the same system model. However, supporting atomic operations such as compare-and-set or increment-and-get in a register makes it equivalent to consensus — so the problems of consensus and a linearizable register are closely related.

questions.question: Give the algorithm for implementing a linearizable compare-and-set using total order broadcast. (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Append a message to the log, tentatively indicating the username you want to claim
Read the log, and wait for the message you appended to be delivered back to you

Check for any messages claiming the username that you want. If the first message for your desired username is your own, then you are successful: you can commit the username claim, perhaps by appending another message to the log, and acknowledge it to the client. If the first message for your desired username is from another user, you abort the operation
Query all of the other nodes before appending, in order to check for concurrent claims to the name

questions.explanation: A footnote notes that if you don't wait but acknowledge the write immediately after it has been enqueued, you get something similar to the memory consistency model of multi-core x86 processors — which is neither linearizable nor sequentially consistent.

questions.question: Why is the append-and-check procedure correct?

options.text: Because all nodes see log entries in the same order
Because the log ordering is established by synchronized clocks
Because each node checks the outcome with every other node
Because the log itself lives on a single designated node

questions.explanation: Shared order plus first-wins gives agreement without further coordination.

questions.question: How can linearizable reads be built on top of a log? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Sequence reads through the log: append a message, read the log, and perform the actual read when the message is delivered back to you — the message's position in the log thus defines the point in time at which the read happens. Quorum reads in etcd work somewhat like this

If the log allows you to fetch the position of the latest log message in a linearizable way, you can query that position, wait for all entries up to that position to be delivered to you, and then perform the read — this is the idea behind ZooKeeper's sync() operation
You can make your read from a replica that is synchronously updated on writes, and is thus sure to be up to date — a technique used in chain replication
You may read from any replica at all, since total order broadcast already guarantees recency

questions.explanation: Three options. The last is wrong because total order broadcast is asynchronous and gives no recency guarantee.

questions.question: To build total order broadcast from linearizable storage, what do you need and what is the algorithm?

options.text: A linearizable register with atomic increment-and-get
You need a synchronized clock and a timestamp per message
You need a version vector per node
You need a single leader, which defeats the purpose

questions.explanation: A linearizable counter gives gapless, agreed sequence numbers.

questions.question: A node has delivered message 4 and receives message 6. What does it do, and what does this illustrate?

options.text: Because the linearizable counter's numbers have no gaps
It delivers message 6 immediately, since order is per-node
It discards message 6 as out of order
It requests message 5 from the sender and then reorders

questions.explanation: Gaplessness is what lets a node know when its order is final.

questions.question: How hard is it to make a linearizable integer with an atomic increment-and-get operation?

options.text: Handling the situation where the node holding the value fails
It is trivial in every case, since a single variable suffices
It is impossible under any of the system models the book has considered so far
It requires nothing more than a synchronized clock

questions.explanation: It is proved that a linearizable compare-and-set (or increment-and-get) register and total order broadcast are both equivalent to consensus: if you can solve one of these problems, you can transform it into a solution for the others. The chapter calls this quite a profound and surprising insight.

questions.question: State the informal goal of consensus and the warning attached to it.

options.text: Getting several nodes to agree on something
The goal is to order all operations; the warning is about performance
The goal is to detect failures; the warning is about clocks
The goal is to replicate data; the warning is about durability

questions.explanation: Deceptively simple, with a long record of broken implementations.

questions.question: Why does consensus appear so late in the book?

options.text: Because the subtleties need the earlier material as prerequisites
Because it matters less than the topics that came before it
Because the algorithms were only invented very recently
Because the author wanted to end the chapter on a hard note

questions.explanation: Five prerequisites, and decades of gradual crystallization even among researchers.

questions.question: Why does single-leader replication need consensus?

options.text: Because all nodes must agree on which node is the leader
Because followers must agree on the order of writes
Because clients must agree on which replica to read from
It doesn't; single-leader replication never needs consensus

questions.explanation: Agreement on leadership identity is the consensus instance here.

questions.question: State the atomic commit problem as an instance of consensus.

options.text: A transaction that may fail on some nodes but succeed on others
Nodes must agree on the isolation level for each transaction
Nodes must agree on the order of writes within a transaction
Nodes must agree on which partition holds each row

questions.explanation: A footnote distinguishes them formally: atomic commit is formalized slightly differently from consensus — an atomic transaction can commit only if all participants vote to commit and must abort if any participant needs to abort, whereas consensus is allowed to decide on any value that is proposed by one of the participants. However, atomic commit and consensus are reducible to each other, and nonblocking atomic commit is harder than consensus.

questions.question: State the FLP result and resolve the apparent contradiction.

options.text: Fischer, Lynch and Paterson — the FLP result
FLP is simply wrong and has been disproved
FLP applies to the partially synchronous model, so consensus is unattainable in practice
FLP applies only to Byzantine faults

questions.explanation: The impossibility is real, and the model it holds in is not the one real systems live in.

questions.question: What is the verdict on two-phase commit, announced before the details?

options.text: That 2PC is the most common solution to atomic commit
That 2PC is the best available consensus algorithm
That 2PC is not a consensus algorithm at all
That 2PC has been superseded and is no longer used

questions.explanation: A consensus algorithm, but not a good one.

questions.question: Describe how a single node implements atomic commit.

options.text: By the storage engine, writing data then a commit record
By taking a lock on every row and releasing it at commit
By writing the commit record first and then the data
By voting among the storage engine's threads

questions.explanation: A single device deciding at a single instant is what makes single-node commit atomic.

questions.question: Give the two examples of multi-node transactions and who supports them.

options.text: A multi-object transaction in a partitioned database
Replication and partitioning; all NoSQL stores support them
Batch and stream processing; only Hadoop supports them
Reads and writes; all databases support them

questions.explanation: Cross-partition writes and global secondary indexes are the two shapes.

questions.question: Why is it not sufficient to send a commit request to all nodes and commit independently on each? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Some nodes may detect a constraint violation or conflict, making an abort necessary, while other nodes are successfully able to commit
Some of the commit requests might be lost in the network, eventually aborting due to a timeout, while other commit requests get through
Some nodes may crash before the commit record is fully written and roll back on recovery, while others successfully commit
The two nodes would deadlock, each one waiting for the other to move first

questions.explanation: If some nodes commit the transaction but others abort it, the nodes become inconsistent with each other, as in Figure 7-3.

questions.question: State the rule about commits and why it holds.

options.text: Only commit once certain that every other node will also commit
A node may commit independently and abort later if needed
Commits are revocable within a bounded window
Commits must be confirmed by a majority before becoming visible

questions.explanation: The chapter concedes one escape: it is possible for the effects of an already-committed transaction to be undone by another, compensating transaction — but from the database's point of view this is a separate transaction, and thus any cross-transaction correctness requirements are the application's problem.

questions.question: Define two-phase commit and where it is exposed.

options.text: An algorithm for atomic commit across multiple nodes
2PC is an isolation level exposed through SQL
2PC is a replication protocol exposed through the replication log
2PC is a locking protocol exposed through FOR UPDATE

questions.explanation: A box warns: two-phase commit (2PC) and two-phase locking are two very different things. 2PC provides atomic commit in a distributed database whereas 2PL provides serializable isolation — they are entirely separate concepts, so ignore the unfortunate similarity in the names.

questions.question: What new component does 2PC introduce, and how is it deployed?

options.text: A coordinator, also called a transaction manager
A quorum of voters, always deployed as a separate cluster
A leader elected among the participants
A message broker between the participants

questions.explanation: Often a library in the application process, which turns out to matter a great deal for availability.

questions.question: Walk the basic 2PC flow.

options.text: Reads and writes on several nodes, which become the participants
The coordinator commits on one node first, then propagates
The participants vote among themselves with no coordinator
The coordinator sends commit requests immediately and aborts later if needed

questions.explanation: Prepare, then decide, then commit or abort.

questions.question: Which everyday ceremony is two-phase commit usually compared to, and where does the analogy break?

options.text: The minister asking bride and groom individually
The minister marries the couple first and asks afterward
Each partner may retract consent at any time
The guests vote on whether the marriage proceeds

questions.explanation: The fainting bit is the analogue of a participant crashing after voting yes.

questions.question: Give the first three steps of the detailed 2PC breakdown. (Select all that apply.)

options.text: When the application wants to begin a distributed transaction, it requests a transaction ID from the coordinator, which is globally unique

The application begins a single-node transaction on each of the participants, and attaches the globally unique transaction ID to it; all reads and writes are done in one of these single-node transactions. If anything goes wrong at this stage, the coordinator or any of the participants can abort

When the application is ready to commit, the coordinator sends a prepare request to all participants, tagged with the global transaction ID; if any of these requests fails or times out, the coordinator sends an abort request for that transaction ID to all participants
The coordinator asks the participants to vote among themselves before phase one of the protocol begins

questions.explanation: Setup, normal work, then the prepare round.

questions.question: Give the last three steps, including the commit point. (Select all that apply.)

options.text: When a participant receives the prepare request, it makes sure that it can definitely commit the transaction under all circumstances — writing all transaction data to disk, since a crash, a power failure, or running out of disk space is not an acceptable excuse for refusing to commit later, and checking for any conflicts or constraint violations. By replying 'yes' it promises to commit the transaction without error if requested, thereby surrendering the right to abort the transaction but without actually committing it

When the coordinator has received responses to all prepare requests, it makes a definitive decision, committing only if all participants voted 'yes'; it must write that decision to its transaction log on disk so that it knows which way it decided in case it subsequently crashes. This is called the commit point

Once the coordinator's decision has been written to disk, the commit or abort request is sent to all participants; if this request fails or times out, the coordinator must retry forever until it succeeds — there is no more going back, and if the decision was to commit, that decision must be enforced no matter how many retries it takes. If a participant has crashed in the meantime, the transaction will be committed when it recovers, since the participant voted 'yes' and cannot refuse to commit when it recovers
If a participant crashes before the commit request reaches it, the coordinator simply aborts the transaction on the remaining nodes and reports failure

questions.explanation: The protocol has two crucial points of no return: when a participant votes 'yes' it promises that it will definitely be able to commit later, even though the coordinator may still choose to abort; and once the coordinator decides, that decision is irrevocable. Those promises ensure the atomicity of 2PC — single-node atomic commit lumps these two events into one, writing the commit record to the transaction log.

questions.question: What are the two cases of coordinator failure, and what is the resulting participant state called?

options.text: Because a participant that voted yes must wait to hear the outcome
Either the coordinator aborts or commits; the state is called pending
Either it fails before or after commit; the state is called blocked
There is only one case; the state is called prepared

questions.explanation: Without hearing from the coordinator the participant has no way of knowing whether the transaction was committed or aborted — in principle the participants could communicate among themselves, but that is not part of the 2PC protocol.

questions.question: A coordinator crashes after some participants have voted. Prove that no unilateral choice by a participant is safe.

options.text: That the coordinator decided to commit before crashing
Both databases received the commit request, so no ambiguity arises
Database 1 can safely abort after a timeout
Database 1 can safely commit after a timeout

questions.explanation: The only way 2PC can complete is by waiting for the coordinator to recover. This is why the coordinator must write its commit or abort decision to a transaction log on disk before sending commit or abort requests: when it recovers, it determines the status of all in-doubt transactions by reading its transaction log, and any transactions that don't have a commit record in the coordinator's log are aborted. Thus the commit point of 2PC comes down to a regular single-node atomic commit on the coordinator.

questions.question: Why is 2PC called a blocking atomic commit protocol, and does 3PC fix it?

options.text: Because it can become stuck waiting for the coordinator to recover
Because it holds locks; 3PC removes the locks and solves the problem
Because it requires unanimity; 3PC requires only a majority
Because it has two phases; 3PC adds a phase and is now standard

questions.explanation: Nonblocking atomic commit requires a perfect failure detector — a reliable mechanism for telling whether a node has crashed or not — and in a network with unbounded delay a timeout is not a reliable failure detector, since a request may time out due to a network problem even if no node has crashed. For this reason 2PC continues to be used, despite the known problem with coordinator failure.

questions.question: Quantify the performance cost of distributed transactions.

options.text: Over 10 times slower than single-node transactions in MySQL
About 10% slower, attributable mainly to the extra network latency
About twice as slow, attributable mainly to lock contention
Not measurably slower, since the extra cost is purely operational

questions.explanation: Many cloud services choose not to implement distributed transactions due to the operational problems they engender: they have a mixed reputation, on the one hand seen as providing an important safety guarantee that would be hard to achieve otherwise, and on the other criticized for causing operational problems, killing performance, and promising more than they can deliver.

questions.question: Name and define the two kinds of distributed transaction the chapter says are often conflated.

options.text: Database-internal ones, as in VoltDB and MySQL Cluster's NDB
Local and remote transactions, distinguished by network hops
Read-only and read-write transactions
Single-partition and cross-partition transactions

questions.explanation: Database-internal transactions do not have to be compatible with any other system, so they can use any protocol and apply optimizations specific to that particular technology — and can often work quite well. On the other hand, transactions spanning heterogeneous technologies are a lot more challenging.

questions.question: Explain how heterogeneous distributed transactions give exactly-once message processing, and what breaks it.

options.text: Acknowledge the message only if the database transaction committed
It works by deduplicating messages at the application level
It works by making all message processing idempotent
It cannot be done at all without a shared transaction log

questions.explanation: The guarantee holds only for participants that speak the same commit protocol.

questions.question: Expand XA, date it, and name its supporting systems.

options.text: X/Open XA, for two-phase commit across heterogeneous technologies
eXtensible Atomic protocol, from 2001, supported only by Java EE containers
X/Open Atomic, from 1981, supported only by mainframe databases
eXactly-once Architecture, from 1999, supported by message brokers only

questions.explanation: XA is not a network protocol — it is merely a C API for interfacing with a transaction coordinator, with bindings in other languages. In Java EE the API is the Java Transaction API (JTA), which in turn is supported by many drivers for databases using JDBC and drivers for message brokers using the JMS APIs.

questions.question: Where does the XA coordinator live, and what happens when the application process dies?

options.text: The coordinator implements the XA API, but its implementation is unspecified
The coordinator runs as a replicated service, so an application crash is harmless
The coordinator runs inside the database, so it survives application crashes
The coordinator is stateless, so no recovery is needed

questions.explanation: A library on the application server's disk becomes a critical piece of durable state.

questions.question: Why can't the rest of the system simply ignore an in-doubt transaction?

options.text: Locking — row-level exclusive locks are held until the outcome is known
Because in-doubt transactions consume memory on the participants
Because in-doubt transactions block replication to followers
They can be ignored, since in-doubt transactions are harmless

questions.explanation: If the coordinator has crashed and takes 20 minutes to start up again, those locks will be held for 20 minutes; and if the coordinator's log is entirely lost for some reason, those locks will be held forever, or at least until the situation is manually resolved by an administrator. While those locks are held no other transaction can modify those rows, and depending on the database other transactions may even be blocked from reading them — so large parts of your application can become unavailable until the in-doubt transaction is resolved.

questions.question: What are orphaned in-doubt transactions, and why doesn't rebooting help?

options.text: Transactions whose outcome the coordinator cannot decide
They are transactions with no participants; rebooting clears them
They are aborted transactions that were never cleaned up; a vacuum process removes them
They are duplicated transactions; deduplication resolves them

questions.explanation: Preserving the locks across restarts is required for correctness, which is exactly why rebooting cannot help.

questions.question: Define heuristic decisions and decode the euphemism.

options.text: Heuristic decisions, letting a participant decide unilaterally
They are optimizations that speed up the common case
They are automatic retries with exponential backoff
They are coordinator elections after a crash

questions.explanation: 'Heuristic' means 'probably breaking atomicity'.

questions.question: What is the 'key realization' about the coordinator, and what limitations follow? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: The transaction coordinator is itself a kind of database — one that stores the outcome of transactions — and so it needs to be approached with the same care as any other important database

If the coordinator is not replicated but runs only on a single machine, it is a single point of failure for the entire system, yet surprisingly many coordinator implementations are not highly available by default or have only rudimentary replication support

Many server-side applications are developed in a stateless model, with all persistent state stored in a database, which has the advantage that application servers can be added and removed at will — but when the coordinator is part of the application server, it changes the nature of the deployment: the coordinator's logs become a crucial part of the durable system state, as important as the databases themselves, since they are required in order to recover in-doubt transactions after a crash. Such application servers are no longer stateless
The coordinator must be co-located with the database in order to reach acceptable performance

questions.explanation: The coordinator is a database, a single point of failure, and a destroyer of statelessness.

questions.question: Give limitations 3 and 4 of XA.

options.text: Because XA must be a lowest common denominator across data systems
XA is too fast for reliable logging, and it requires special hardware
XA cannot support more than two participants, and it requires synchronized clocks
XA requires Byzantine fault tolerance, and it forbids replication

questions.explanation: For database-internal distributed transactions the limitations are not so great — a distributed version of SSI is possible, for example. However, there remains the problem that for 2PC to commit, all participants must respond. The chapter notes there are alternative methods that achieve the same thing without the pain of heterogeneous distributed transactions, returning to them in Chapters 11 and 12.

questions.question: Give the informal and formal statements of consensus.

options.text: Getting several nodes to agree on something
Formally, all nodes must propose the same value and the algorithm confirms it
Formally, the algorithm invents a new value not proposed by anyone
Formally, each node decides independently and they are later reconciled

questions.explanation: Proposals in, one decision out.

questions.question: Name and define the four properties a consensus algorithm must satisfy. (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Uniform agreement: no two nodes decide differently
Integrity: no node decides twice
Validity: if a node decides value v, then v must have been proposed by a majority of nodes
Termination: every node that does not crash eventually decides some value

questions.explanation: Validity requires only that v was proposed by some node, not by a majority — that weaker form is what makes the property implementable. The chapter notes this is the formalization of 'uniform consensus', equivalent to regular consensus in asynchronous systems with unreliable failure detectors — and that the literature usually refers to processes rather than nodes, but the book uses nodes for consistency.
