questions.question: Which properties define the core idea of consensus, and what is validity actually for?

options.text: Everyone decides the same outcome, and a decision is irrevocable
Termination and validity are the core; agreement rules out trivial solutions
Validity is the core; agreement is an optimization
All four of the properties are equally core, so the chapter draws no distinction between them

questions.explanation: If you don't care about fault tolerance, satisfying the first three properties is easy: you can just hardcode one node to be the 'dictator' and let that node make all of the decisions — but if that one node fails, the system can no longer make any decisions. This is, in fact, what we saw in the case of two-phase commit: if the coordinator fails, in-doubt participants cannot decide whether to commit or abort.

questions.question: What does termination formalize, and which algorithm fails it?

options.text: Fault tolerance — an algorithm must eventually reach a decision
Termination formalizes safety; 2PC satisfies it
Termination formalizes ordering; Paxos fails it
Termination formalizes durability; no algorithm fails it

questions.explanation: Liveness, with a crash-stop assumption that rules out waiting for recovery.

questions.question: How many nodes must survive for consensus?

options.text: That a majority of nodes must be working for progress to be possible
At least one node, which is then able to decide alone
Every node must survive for any decision to be made
At least two-thirds of the nodes, in the non-Byzantine case

questions.explanation: Most implementations ensure that the safety properties — agreement, integrity and validity — are always met, even if a majority of nodes fail or there is a severe network problem: so a large-scale outage can stop the system from being able to process requests, but it cannot corrupt the consensus system by causing it to make invalid decisions.

questions.question: What fault model do most consensus algorithms assume, and what is the bound for the harder model?

options.text: That there are no Byzantine faults
They assume Byzantine faults, tolerating up to one-half faulty nodes
They assume no faults at all
They assume crash-stop faults with no bound

questions.explanation: Non-Byzantine by default, with a one-third bound if you want Byzantine tolerance.

questions.question: Name the best-known fault-tolerant consensus algorithms, and what do they actually decide?

options.text: Viewstamped Replication, Paxos, Raft and Zab
Only Paxos and Raft, which decide a single value each time
2PC and 3PC, which decide commit or abort
Gossip and anti-entropy, which decide replica state

questions.explanation: Viewstamped Replication, Raft and Zab implement total order broadcast directly, because that is more efficient than doing repeated rounds of one-value-at-a-time consensus; in the case of Paxos this optimization is known as Multi-Paxos. The chapter advises against implementing a consensus system yourself — which is probably not advisable, it's hard.

questions.question: Map the four consensus properties onto the total order broadcast guarantees they produce. (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Agreement: all nodes decide to deliver the same messages in the same order
Integrity: messages are not duplicated
Validity: messages are not corrupted and not fabricated out of thin air
Termination: every message is delivered within a bounded time after being sent

questions.explanation: Total order broadcast makes no timing promise. Termination corresponds to messages not being lost. A clean one-to-one mapping between consensus properties and broadcast guarantees.

questions.question: Why didn't Chapter 5 need consensus, and what conundrum does automatic failover create?

options.text: How the leader is chosen
Chapter 5 used consensus implicitly through quorums
Automatic failover avoids consensus entirely
Manual failover satisfies termination

questions.explanation: The apparent circularity is resolved by epoch numbers.

questions.question: What weaker guarantee do the protocols make about leaders, and what is the epoch number called in each algorithm?

options.text: They use epoch numbers, guaranteeing a unique leader per epoch
They guarantee a unique leader at all times; the number is the sequence number
They guarantee no leader; the number is the round number
The epoch number is called the zxid in all three

questions.explanation: Uniqueness per epoch rather than globally is what breaks the circularity.

questions.question: How do epoch numbers advance, and what is the tie-break rule?

options.text: An election with a monotonically increasing epoch number
Epoch numbers are assigned randomly, and the lower one prevails
Epoch numbers come from wall-clock time, and the later one prevails
Epoch numbers never change once assigned

questions.explanation: Monotonic epochs with higher-wins resolution.

questions.question: Why can't a node simply trust that it is the leader?

options.text: Because a node cannot trust its own judgment about being leader
Because a leader is elected purely by its timestamp
Because leadership is transferred on every single write
It can trust itself, since leadership is self-certifying

questions.explanation: Majority acceptance, not self-assertion, is what confers leadership.

questions.question: Walk the quorum-overlap argument.

options.text: Two rounds of voting: one for the leader, one for its proposal
The two quorums must be disjoint in order to avoid bias
Only a single round of voting is actually needed
Both of the quorums are required to be unanimous

questions.explanation: Overlap is what lets a successful proposal vote certify continued leadership.

questions.question: How does epoch voting differ from two-phase commit? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: In 2PC the coordinator is not elected
Fault-tolerant consensus algorithms only require votes from a majority of nodes, whereas 2PC requires a 'yes' vote from every participant
Consensus algorithms define a recovery process by which nodes can get into a consistent state after a new leader is elected, ensuring that the safety properties are always met
2PC relies on epoch numbers whereas consensus algorithms manage without them

questions.explanation: These differences are key to the correctness and fault tolerance of a consensus algorithm.

questions.question: What do consensus algorithms deliver, and what are the first two costs?

options.text: Concrete safety properties where everything else is uncertain
They provide eventual consistency with no majority requirement
They require only two nodes to tolerate one failure
They are fully asynchronous with no replication cost

questions.explanation: Safety plus fault tolerance, paid for in synchronous voting and majority quorums.

questions.question: Give the remaining limitations of consensus algorithms. (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Static membership: most consensus algorithms assume a fixed set of nodes that participate in voting, which means you can't just add or remove nodes in the cluster. Dynamic membership extensions allow the set of nodes to change over time, but they are much less well understood than static membership algorithms

Timeout sensitivity: consensus systems rely on timeouts to detect failed nodes, and in environments with highly variable network delays — especially geographically distributed systems — it often happens that a node falsely believes the leader to have failed due to a transient network issue. Although this error does not harm the safety properties, frequent leader elections result in terrible performance, because the system can end up spending more time choosing a leader than doing any useful work

Network-fault sensitivity: Raft in particular has been shown to have unpleasant edge cases — if the entire network is working correctly except for one particular network link that is consistently unreliable, Raft can get into situations where leadership continually bounces between two nodes, or the current leader is continually forced to resign, so the system effectively never makes progress
Byzantine sensitivity: a consensus algorithm breaks down as soon as any node is merely slow to respond

questions.explanation: Three further limitations: membership, timeouts and pathological link failures. Other consensus algorithms have been designed to be more robust to unreliable networks.

questions.question: How are ZooKeeper and etcd usually described, and what should you ask about that description?

options.text: Distributed key-value stores, or coordination and configuration services
They are described as message brokers; the question is about ordering
They are described as relational databases; the question is about SQL
They are described as caches; the question is about eviction

questions.explanation: You rarely need to use ZooKeeper directly, since it is actually not well suited as a general-purpose database — it's more likely that you will end up relying on it indirectly via some other project, for example HBase, Hadoop YARN, OpenStack Nova and Kafka all rely on ZooKeeper running in the background.

questions.question: What is ZooKeeper's data-size design point, and how is it replicated?

options.text: Small amounts of data that fit entirely in memory
They hold terabytes on disk, replicated by quorum writes
They hold data in memory only, with no durability
They hold arbitrary data, replicated asynchronously

questions.explanation: ZooKeeper is modeled after Google's Chubby lock service and implements not only total order broadcast, and hence consensus, but also an interesting set of other features that turn out to be particularly useful when building distributed systems: linearizable atomic operations, total ordering of operations, failure detection and change notifications.

questions.question: Which primitive gives you a lock, and under what conditions does the guarantee hold?

options.text: An atomic compare-and-set, which lets only one node win
A read-write register, guaranteed only when the network is healthy
A timestamp comparison, guaranteed only with synchronized clocks
A quorum read, guaranteed only with strict quorums

questions.explanation: Compare-and-set is exactly the operation that requires consensus.

questions.question: Why do you need a fencing token, and how does ZooKeeper supply it?

options.text: A fencing token, to stop clients conflicting at the resource
Tokens prevent replay attacks; ZooKeeper uses cryptographic nonces
Tokens identify clients; ZooKeeper uses session IDs
Tokens are not needed with leases

questions.explanation: Monotonic ordering of all operations is what makes zxid a valid fencing token.

questions.question: Describe the ZooKeeper session and failure detection mechanism.

options.text: Long-lived sessions kept alive by periodic heartbeats
Clients poll on every operation; there is no session concept
The server pings clients once per hour; locks are never released automatically
Sessions end immediately on any connection interruption

questions.explanation: Sessions survive transient interruption but not sustained heartbeat loss.

questions.question: What can a client do beyond reading another client's values?

options.text: Watching keys for changes, so clients learn when they change
It can only poll, since watches are not supported at all
It can subscribe, but only to keys that it created itself
It receives notifications only when its session ends

questions.explanation: Of ZooKeeper's four features, only the linearizable atomic operations really require consensus — however, it is the combination of these features that makes systems like ZooKeeper so useful for distributed coordination.

questions.question: Where does the ZooKeeper and Chubby model work well? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Allocating work to nodes: if you have several instances of a process or service and one of them needs to be chosen as leader or primary, and if the leader fails one of the other nodes should take over — useful for single-leader databases but also for job schedulers and similar stateful systems
Deciding which partition to assign to which node when you have some partitioned resource — a database, message streams, file storage, distributed actor system and so on

Rebalancing: as new nodes join the cluster some partitions need to be moved from existing nodes to the new nodes in order to rebalance the load, and as nodes are removed or fail other nodes need to take over the failed nodes' work
Storing the application's primary dataset, for the sake of durability

questions.explanation: These tasks can be achieved by judicious use of atomic operations, ephemeral nodes and notifications in ZooKeeper — and if done correctly, this approach allows the application to automatically recover from faults without human intervention. It's not easy, despite the appearance of libraries such as Apache Curator that provide higher-level tools on top of the ZooKeeper client API, but it is still much better than attempting to implement the necessary consensus algorithms from scratch, which has a poor success record.

questions.question: An application grows to thousands of nodes. Why can't the coordination mechanism grow with it?

options.text: Because majority votes over that many nodes would be too inefficient
Because ZooKeeper has a hard limit of 100 nodes
Because clients cannot connect to more than three nodes
It can grow; ZooKeeper scales its voting set with the cluster

questions.explanation: A small fixed voting set serving many clients is the architectural answer.

questions.question: What kind of data belongs in ZooKeeper, and what doesn't?

options.text: Slow-changing data, such as which node is the current leader
High-frequency runtime state belongs in ZooKeeper; slow-changing metadata does not
Both kinds belong in ZooKeeper
Neither kind of data belongs in ZooKeeper, which stores only locks

questions.explanation: Minutes-to-hours metadata, not millions-per-second state.

questions.question: Does service discovery require consensus?

options.text: Service discovery
Yes, service discovery strictly requires linearizability
No, and neither does leader election
Yes, because IP addresses must be unique

questions.explanation: Although service discovery does not require consensus, leader election does — so if your consensus system already knows who the leader is, it can make sense to also use that information to help other services discover who the leader is. For this purpose some consensus systems support read-only caching replicas, which asynchronously receive the log of all decisions of the consensus algorithm but do not actively participate in voting, and are therefore able to serve read requests that do not need to be linearizable.

questions.question: Define a membership service and explain how it gets around the Chapter 8 obstacle.

options.text: Which nodes are currently active and live members of the cluster
A membership service detects failures perfectly using timeouts
A membership service avoids consensus by using gossip
A membership service requires synchronized clocks

questions.explanation: Agreement without accuracy is still valuable. Research into membership services goes back to the 1980s and has been important for building highly reliable systems, for example for air traffic control.

questions.question: Which problems are equivalent to consensus? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Linearizable compare-and-set registers, which must atomically decide whether to set their value based on whether the current value equals the parameter given in the operation; and atomic transaction commit, where a database must decide whether to commit or abort a distributed transaction
Total order broadcast, where the messaging system must decide on the order in which to deliver messages

Locks and leases, where when several clients are racing to grab a lock or lease the lock decides which one successfully acquired it; and membership/coordination service, where given a failure detector such as timeouts the system must decide which nodes are alive and which should be considered dead because their sessions timed out
Uniqueness constraint, where concurrent transactions creating the same key must all be rejected in order to keep the system safe

questions.explanation: One of them must be allowed to succeed — the constraint decides which, rather than rejecting them all. The remaining two equivalent problems are atomic transaction commit and membership/coordination services. Six problems, equivalent in the sense that if you have a solution for one of them, you can easily transform it into a solution for one of the others. Achieving consensus means deciding something in such a way that all nodes agree on what was decided, and such that the decision is irrevocable.

questions.question: Under what conditions are all six problems straightforward?

options.text: They are straightforward on a single node, or with a single decider
When a majority of the nodes agree, with no leader needed
When clocks are synchronized to within a millisecond
When the underlying network is reliable enough

questions.explanation: Vesting decisions in one node makes them easy and makes that node a single point of failure.

questions.question: Give the three ways to handle leader failure and the objections. (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Wait for the leader to recover, and accept that the system will be blocked in the meantime — many XA/JTA transaction coordinators choose this option. But it does not fully solve consensus because it does not satisfy the termination property: if the leader does not recover, the system can be blocked forever

Manually fail over by getting humans to choose a new leader node and reconfigure the system to use it — an option taken by many relational databases. It is a kind of consensus by 'act of God', since the human operator outside of the computer system makes the decision, and the speed of failover is limited by the speed at which humans can act, which is generally slower than computers
Use an algorithm to automatically choose a new leader, which requires a consensus algorithm — and it is advisable to use a proven algorithm that correctly handles adverse network conditions
Allow multiple leaders and resolve the resulting conflicts afterwards, which fully solves the consensus problem

questions.explanation: Wait, human, or algorithm — and only the third satisfies termination.

questions.question: A single-leader database provides linearizability without running consensus on every write. So why does it still require consensus?

options.text: Because it still needs consensus to elect a leader and handle failover
It does not require consensus at any point during its operation
It requires consensus on every write, contrary to the claim
It requires consensus for its reads but never for its writes

questions.explanation: Consensus relocated and made rare, not eliminated. In order to elect a leader, we first need a leader.

questions.question: What role do tools like ZooKeeper play for an application?

options.text: An 'outsourced' consensus, failure detection and membership service
As a general-purpose database that replaces relational systems
As a message broker for high-throughput streams
As a library you should reimplement yourself for your use case

questions.explanation: Hard to use, much better than the alternative of rolling your own.
